articles.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio may be looking to quit the Trump administration and run for presidency in 2028, a report by The Independent said. US midterm elections were disastrous for Republicans as they lost control of both the House and the Senate. Rubio needs to distance himself from controversial policies of Trump administration like US Iran war, the report said citing insiders. The move may help to improve his prospects in the 2028 Republican presidential nomination against main rival US Vice President J. D. Vance.Marco Rubio ResignationUS secretary of state and White House national security adviser seems to be looking for an early exit from President Donald Trump's cabinet to lay the groundwork for a 2028 Republican presidential run, The Independent report said citing unnamed party insiders and sources. Rubio may need to distance himself from the Trump administration to avoid the fallout of foreign policy issues like US Iran war, the sources said.Who will exit Trump administration?Around five cabinet members are looking to exit the administration to avoid congressional investigations or impeachment efforts under a newly elected Democratic majority, the report said citing insiders. The White House and the State Department have strongly denied the report. The speculation of the departures has been dismissed and called baseless.The speculation comes after devastating US midterm results for Republicans as they lost control of both the House and the Senate. White House spokesperson Davis Ingle dismissed the claims as "baseless, false conspiracy theories," an Anadolu Agency report said. State Department Assistant Secretary Dylan Johnson characterized the reports as "completely baseless fake news from made-up anonymous 'sources'".J. D. Vance may be his main rivalVice President J. D. Vance may be currently his main rival in the race to be the Republican nominee in November 2028, the report said citing senior party sources in the US and senior figures in the UK government.Vice president JD Vance has already blamed the war in Iran for the disastrous results to distance himself from it. Trump may also pin the blame for the policy and US midterm election loss on Rubio, defense secretary Pete Hegseth and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles. These all the officials may be the potential scapegoats, the report said.

Wall Street, however, still sees considerable upside in the stock.NVDA Stock Price Falls TodayNvidia shares fell more than 6% to around $186 in early trading Thursday. If the decline holds, it would be the first time the stock has closed below $200 since July 30, according to Barron's.The concern is that fewer data center projects could eventually mean fewer orders for Nvidia's processors and networking equipment. Companies such as SpaceX and CoreWeave are already facing investor concerns over possible construction delays, putting pressure on shares of businesses closely tied to the AI infrastructure expansion.However, delayed projects do not necessarily mean that spending will disappear. Technology companies could shift construction to other states or overseas. Gavekal US chief economist Will Denyer told Barron's that some states and counties would remain willing to welcome data centers because of the tax revenue they bring.135579574135576908Nvidia Stock Price Today Faces Pressure Despite Strong Revenue GrowthThe latest decline comes at a time when Nvidia's business continues to grow rapidly. The company has forecast 70% revenue growth for fiscal 2028, largely corresponding to calendar 2027, and has indicated that supply constraints, rather than a lack of demand, are limiting its growth.Nvidia generated $96.22 billion in revenue in its latest quarter, up 105.8% from a year earlier. It also recorded its fifth consecutive earnings beat. Its third quarter revenue guidance stands at $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, assuming no data center compute revenue from China.The chipmaker closed Wednesday at $200.13, down 3.17%, after touching an intraday low of $199.68. The decline came even as S&P 500 gained 1.58% and the Nasdaq Composite advanced 1.44%.The stock is now about 16.3% below its October 6 record closing price of $239.24 and trades below its 50-day and 200-day moving averages, according to 24/7 Wall St report.135575113NVDA Stock Could Rebound as Analysts Maintain Bullish TargetsDespite the recent selling, Wall Street analysts remain optimistic about Nvidia. FactSet data cited by Barron's puts the average price target at approximately $333. articles.title: US jobless claims hit 57-year low
articles.summary: WASHINGTON: The number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment slipped to a 57-year last week as layoffs remained low against the backdrop of a resilient labor market.Initial claims for state unemployment benefits fell 6,000 to a seasonally adjusted 189,000 for the week ended October 31, the Labor Department said on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 196,000 claims for the latest week.Claims matched the 189,000 level touched in mid-July, which was the lowest reading since 1969.They have stayed mostly below 200,000 since mid-September.Low layoffs, thanks to strong domestic demand and profit growth, are anchoring the labor market, with hiring still constrained by uncertainty over the dragging US-Israeli war with Iran.The government reported this week that there were 1.06 open jobs for every unemployed person in September, up from 1.02 in August, which some economists argued was a sign of the labor market starting to tighten. Others, however, viewed the low level of jobless claims as a function of a smaller labor force amid an immigration crackdown, rather than fewer job cuts.A separate report from global outplacement firm Challenger, Gray and Christmas on Thursday showed US-based employers announced 43,994 job cuts in October, up 2% from September. Planned layoffs dropped 71% compared to October 2025.Despite the rise over the month, layoffs were the lowest for any October since 2023. Employers announced plans to hire 444,692 workers last month, a 57% jump from October 2025. Hiring plans were the highest for any October since 2009, and likely mostly seasonal jobs."Employers are holding on to the workers they have heading into the holidays, and the hiring they are announcing is largely short-term, seasonal work," said Andy Challenger, chief revenue officer at Challenger, Gray & Christmas. "Companies want the flexibility to meet holiday demand without adding permanent headcount."The reluctance to increase permanent hiring means some unemployed people are experiencing long periods of joblessness.The claims report showed the number of people receiving unemployment benefits after an initial week of aid, a proxy for hiring, increased 23,000 to a still-low seasonally adjusted 1.718 million during the week ended October 24. The so-called continuing claims, however, do not include some unemployed people, including recent college graduates and others who have little or no work history.Some people might also have exhausted their eligibility for benefits, limited to 26 weeks in most states, keeping continuing claims at relatively low levels.The claims report has no bearing on the government's closely watched employment report for October due on Friday as it falls outside the survey period. Nonfarm payrolls likely increased by 65,000 jobs last month after rising 29,000 in September, a Reuters survey of economists showed. The unemployment rate is forecast unchanged at 4.2

articles.title: Mahindra realty arm buys 100 acres in Bom
articles.summary: Mahindra Lifespace Developers, the real estate and infrastructure development arm of the Mahindra Group, has acquired 100 acres of land along the Karjat-Murbad road in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region (MMR) for a plotted development project, marking its entry into the segment in the region.The company is likely to start the project around the middle of the next financial year. It is also looking to acquire additional land in the area, according to people familiar with the development.The land acquisition is part of Mahindra Lifespace Developers’ efforts to expand its residential development pipeline across key markets. The company has been pursuing projects through outright land acquisitions, joint development agreements and partnerships with landowners.“In line with our strategy, we look to expand into plotted development in future in MMR, Pune and Bengaluru. Homebuyers today are increasingly seeking greater flexibility and personalization in their residential requirements. Plotted developments offer a compelling proposition through land ownership, customization, and long-term appreciation potential,” said Vimalendra Singh, Chief Business Officer - Residential, Mahindra Lifespace Developers.The proposed development will be the company’s first plotted project outside Mahindra World City in Chennai. In Chennai, Mahindra Lifespace Developers has established a presence in the segment through two projects.The Mumbai-region project marks the company’s entry into a segment that has attracted interest from homebuyers seeking land ownership and the option of building independent homes.Plotted developments have emerged as an alternative to conventional residential projects, with homebuyers showing interest in owning land and having the flexibility to construct homes according to their requirements.Developers are also looking at plotted projects as a way to enter markets where large land parcels are available, without undertaking construction of apartment buildings. The format allows developers to sell individual plots in phases, while buyers can decide the timing and design of construction, subject to applicable regulations.Several developers have been exploring plotted development opportunities as part of their residential portfolios, particularly in locations on the outskirts of major cities, attracting institutional capital and investments from real estate funds into land acquisition and development projects.

articles.title: LIC Q2 Results: Profit jumps 20% YoY to Rs 12,115 crore, NPI grows 16%
articles.summary: Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC), the country's largest insurer, reported a nearly 20% rise in consolidated net profit to Rs 12,114.78 crore for the September quarter on Thursday, supported by strong growth in premium income and higher investment earnings. The state-owned insurer had reported a net profit of Rs 10,098 crore in the corresponding quarter last year. However, profit declined 11% sequentially from Rs 13,584 crore in the June quarter.Net premium income increased 16.2% year-on-year to Rs 1.47 lakh crore from Rs 1.26 lakh crore in the September quarter of FY26. It rose 15% sequentially from Rs 1.27 lakh crore.The growth in premium income was largely driven by a sharp increase in single-premium collections, reflecting higher contributions from policies where customers pay the entire premium upfront.Single-premium income surged 34% to Rs 68,425 crore from Rs 50,882 crore a year earlier. Renewal premium income increased 5% to Rs 68,718 crore from Rs 65,320 crore in the same quarter last year. However, first-year premium income declined 4% to Rs 10,484 crore from Rs 10,884 crore.LIC also reported an increase in investment income during the quarter, providing additional support to profitability.Net investment income in the shareholders' account increased to Rs 2,855 crore from Rs 2,066 crore a year earlier, representing a rise of about 38%.Total income in the shareholders' account increased 11% to Rs 10,527 crore from Rs 9,454 crore. Meanwhile, the insurer's income from investments in the policyholders' account stood at Rs 1.15 lakh crore, compared with Rs 1.12 lakh crore in the year-ago quarter, an increase of around 2.2%.The company reported a surplus of Rs 10,379 crore in the policyholders' account, compared with Rs 9,503 crore a year earlier. The increase in investment income and policyholder surplus contributed to the company's overall financial performance during the quarter.LIC's benefits paid, including claims and other policyholder payouts, increased to Rs 1.34 lakh crore from Rs 1.06 lakh crore in the corresponding quarter last year.Expenses of management rose to Rs 15,143.38 crore from Rs 13,908 crore, an increase of 9%. Net commission expenses increased to Rs 6,089 crore from Rs 5,807 crore a year earlier.LIC's solvency ratio improved to 2.35 as of September 2026, from 2.13 a year earlier. However, the ratio declined sequentially from 2.42 in the June quarter. The insurer's expense of management ratio improved to 10.26% from 12.05% a year earlier, reflecting better cost efficiency.The 13th-month persistency ratio declined to 67.67% from 68.19% a year earlier, while the 25th-month ratio improved marginally to 63.01% from 62.63%.The insurer's investment yield, excluding unrealised gains, declined to 9.04% in the September quarter from 9.33% a year earlier. However, including unrealised gains, the yield increased to 4.10% from 2.07%.

Mistry challenges removal as SDTT trustee
articles.summary: New Delhi: Mehli Mistry has challenged his removal as a trustee of Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT) and Bai Hirabai Jamsetji Tata Navsari Charitable Institution before the Maharashtra Charity Commissioner, alleging procedural irregularities and violations of trust governance rules.In three rejoinders and applications filed before the Deputy Charity Commissioner, Mistry has questioned the legality of the decisions leading to his removal, the eligibility of certain trustees and their participation in decisions concerning his reappointment.He has also sought an independent inquiry into SDTT's administration, alleging conflicts of interest, improper retention of financial benefits by trustees and irregularities in decisions involving Tata Group companies and the trust's investments in Tata Sons.A key issue raised by Mistry concerns Venu Srinivasan's participation in the decision on his reappointment. Mistry has argued that Srinivasan's tenure as a trustee ended on October 23, 2025, while he communicated his vote against Mistry's reappointment on October 28.Read more: Tata Sons Chairman Chandrasekaran meets Italian PM Meloni after Iveco acquisitionAccording to Mistry, the trust's own records acknowledged that Srinivasan was no longer a trustee when he cast his vote. He has pointed out that a footnote in the records stated that Srinivasan's vote should be disregarded for this reason.However, Mistry contends that removing the vote from the final count does not address the larger issue, as Srinivasan was still included in the decision-making process. He has argued that the entire resolution was invalid because the body considering his reappointment was not properly constituted.Mistry has also disputed the trust's position that his three-year tenure ended on October 28, 2025, requiring a fresh resolution for reappointment. He has cited the SDTT Trust Deed of March 11, 1932, arguing that it does not prescribe a fixed tenure for trustees.He has further relied on an October 17, 2024, joint resolution of SDTT and Sir Ratan Tata Trust, which provided for the reappointment of trustees after the expiry of their tenure without any limitation on the renewed term, subject to applicable law.Read more: Finance Minister Sitharaman urges Tata to resolve feud amicably, rules out govt interventionIn a separate challenge concerning the Bai Hirabai Jamsetji Tata Navsari Charitable Institution, Mistry has questioned the eligibility of trustees under the trust deed. He has cited provisions requiring trustees to profess the Parsi Zoroastrian faith and meet specified residency conditions.On this basis, he has questioned the eligibility of Venu Srinivasan and Vijay Singh. He has also raised questions about Noel Tata's alleged Irish citizenship and UAE residency, arguing that eligibility requirements should be applied uniformly to all trustees.Mistry has sought affidavits from trustees confirming that they meet the qualifications prescribed under the trust deed. He has also disputed the trust's position that the relevant eligibility provisions are invalid or unenforceable.Separately, Mistry has sought an inquiry into the financial affairs of SDTT, particularly commissions and other benefits allegedly received by trustees serving as nominee directors in Tata Group companies.His application refers to an annual commission of approximately Rs 1.42 crore received by Noel Tata from Tata Sons Private Limited during FY 2024-25, as reflected in corporate filings.He has also raised questions concerning the engagement of Gerry McGovern for Norton Motorcycles, equity infusion into Tata International Limited and alleged deviations from unanimous resolutions on voting the trust's shareholding in Tata Sons.Mistry has argued that such matters could involve conflicts of interest and breaches of fiduciary duties. He has urged the Charity Commissioner to examine corporate filings, declarations of interest, board records and relevant approvals.He has sought rejection of SDTT's preliminary objections and an inquiry or inspection under the Maharashtra Public Trusts Act, 1950.Importantly, Mistry has clarified that he is not seeking reinstatement as an SDTT trustee. Instead, he has sought an examination of the trust's administration and the appointment of an independent administrator, if required, to ensure its proper functioning.Mistry's trusteeship of SDTT and Sir Ratan Tata Trust ended in October 2025 after three trustees opposed his reappointment. On November 4, 2025, he had written to Tata Trusts trustees, including chairman Noel Tata, describing his departure as a harmonious exit and saying he did not wish to drag the charitable institutions into controversy.In the letter, he stressed the need to protect the reputation of the institutions and uphold transparency, good governance and public interest. He also cited a quote attributed to the late Ratan Tata: "Nobody is bigger than the institution it serves."Mistry had earlier filed a caveat before the Maharashtra Charity Commissioner, seeking an opportunity to be heard before any changes were made to the register of trustees.

articles.title: Bharti Airtel Q2 Results: Net profit jumps 31% YoY to Rs 8,887 crore; revenue up 17%; ARPU rises to Rs 271
articles.summary: Bharti Airtel reported a 31% year-on-year (YoY) increase in net profit to Rs 8,887.5 crore for the September quarter (Q2FY27), compared with Rs 6,791.6 crore in the corresponding quarter last fiscal.The telecom major's consolidated revenue for the quarter rose 16.7% YoY to Rs 60,878 crore, up from Rs 52,145 crore reported in Q2FY26.India mobile revenue grew 10.1% YoY, while ARPU increased to Rs 271 in Q2FY27 from Rs 256 in the year-ago quarter, reflecting improved customer realisations.Operating performance remained strong, with earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) growing 17.8% YoY to Rs 35,240 crore in Q2FY27, compared with Rs 29,919 crore in the year-ago period.India revenue increased 9.4% YoY to Rs 42,308 crore, with the company's mobile business continuing to benefit from premiumisation of its customer portfolio, higher average revenue per user (ARPU) and strong additions in smartphone data customers.The company's Homes business remained another key growth driver, with revenue increasing 25.3% YoY. The segment added 676,000 customers during the quarter, taking its total customer base to 15.4 million.Airtel Business reported an 11.4% YoY increase in revenue, driven by broad-based growth across its core connectivity business and digital services portfolio. Digital TV revenue rose 2.4% YoY to Rs 771 crore, supported by growing adoption of IPTV services.Africa continued to deliver strong growth, with revenue increasing 25.7% YoY in reported currency and 20.6% in constant currency. The business had a customer base of 193.9 million.Airtel's balance sheet also strengthened during the quarter. Its consolidated net debt-to-EBITDA ratio, on an annualised basis, improved to 1.18 from 1.63 as of September 30, 2025. The net debt-to-EBITDAaL ratio, excluding lease obligations, stood at 0.70.The company reported consolidated capital expenditure of Rs 12,467 crore during the quarter, including Rs 9,908 crore in India. It also invested Rs 2,826 crore in a strategic land parcel for its data centre expansion plans in the country.Postpaid additions hit record; smartphone data base expandsOn the operational front, Airtel added 2.9 million smartphone data customers sequentially, taking the number of such users to 81% of its overall mobile customer base. Smartphone data customer additions stood at 18.8 million over the past year.The postpaid segment recorded net additions of 1.2 million customers during the quarter, its strongest-ever performance in a single quarter, taking the overall postpaid base to 31.2 million.Mobile data consumption increased 36.5% YoY to 36.5 GB per customer per month.The company added 497 towers and 11,684 mobile broadband base stations during the quarter. Its network expansion over the past year included 5,649 additional towers and 44,718 kilometres of fibre.Across its operations in 15 countries, Airtel's total customer base expanded to 693 million, supported by quarterly net additions of 12 million customers across India and Africa.Management commentaryCommenting on the performance, Gopal Vittal, Executive Vice Chairman of Bharti Airtel, said the company delivered another quarter of consistent growth, supported by its diversified business portfolio.He highlighted Africa's strong performance, with revenue growing 6.7% sequentially in constant currency, attributing the improvement partly to the deployment of Airtel's homegrown technology stack across markets. India business revenue also recorded healthy sequential growth of 2.7%.Vittal said the India mobile business continued to benefit from the company's portfolio premiumisation strategy and focus on acquiring quality customers. The segment recorded 3.4% sequential revenue growth, while postpaid additions touched a record 1.2 million during the quarter.He also pointed to sustained momentum in the Homes business, which added 676,000 customers, and Airtel Business, which reported 3.8% sequential revenue growth.The company's newer growth initiatives, including financial services and data centres, are also gaining traction, Vittal said. Airtel's investment in a strategic land parcel during the quarter is part of its ambition to build 1 GW of data centre capacity.He added that the company remained focused on maintaining a strong balance sheet, supported by robust cash generation and disciplined capital allocation.Bharti Airtel shares end lowerShares of Bharti Airtel ended Thursday's trading session 0.52% lower at Rs 2,056.90, compared with the previous close of Rs 2,067.60 on the NSE.During the session, the stock traded in a range of Rs 2,048-2,084.The telecom major's shares have declined nearly 3% so far this year. At the prevailing market price, Bharti Airtel had a market capitalisation of approximately Rs 12.84 lakh crore.

AI, data, cyber lead tech hiring at 30.3%
articles.summary: AI, data and cybersecurity represented 30.3% of tech hiring demand in the July–September quarter, up from 25.8% in the preceding quarter, according to a report by staffing and workforce solutions company Quess Corp.India’s global capability centres (GCCs) are directing a greater share of their technology recruitment towards specialists who can deploy AI, manage data and secure enterprise systems, the India GCC Tech Talent Landscape Q2 FY27 report said.Demand for AI, data and analytics professionals grew approximately 14% quarter-on-quarter, while that for cybersecurity and risk management roles increased approximately 12%. Both categories expanded even as overall GCC tech hiring demand declined 3.5%, reflecting continued investment in specialist capabilities within more selective workforce plans.The moderation in demand is consistent with the cyclical hiring patterns of global enterprises, where recruitment typically peaks at the beginning of the calendar year and slows towards year-end.“India’s GCC ecosystem continues to expand, but its growth is also changing the skills companies need,” said Kapil Joshi, CEO – IT staffing at Quess Corp.“As centres expand their responsibilities and explore new talent markets, companies will need to combine specialist hiring with reskilling and internal mobility. This will help them build the capabilities needed to support their growing role in global operations,” Joshi said.Technology and product GCCs recorded the highest share of postings requiring AI and GenAI skills at approximately 32%. Pharma and healthcare saw a five percentage-point increase to approximately 23%, while professional services and consulting rose four percentage points to approximately 22%. Telecom and networks, manufacturing and industrial, and BFSI recorded quarter-on-quarter declines in overall tech hiring demand of approximately 24%, 9% and 8%, respectively.The proportion of postings seeking AI and GenAI skills increased in each industry segment, showing that high-skill roles are gaining importance.Demand within advanced skill clusters also points towards the practical deployment of AI. Applied data science and model operations grew approximately 19%, while cloud security and AI-infused architecture increased approximately 21%. These roles support the deployment, monitoring and management of AI models, alongside secure cloud and enterprise infrastructure.The report estimates a 38–42% supply gap in AI, data and analytics and a 30–35% gap in cybersecurity and risk management.It identified pathways to address these shortages through transitions from adjacent roles, including data scientists moving into model operations, data engineers into applied AI, and cybersecurity analysts into cloud security. Structured reskilling and internal career pathways can complement external recruitment as AI requirements deepen across sectors.Tier-1 cities nevertheless account for approximately 87–88% of advanced-skill hiring and 84–86% of total GCC hiring demand in the country, the report said. But smaller cities are growing faster.Coimbatore stood out with approximately 30% quarter-on-quarter growth in GCC tech hiring demand, helping drive overall tier-2 growth of approximately 13%, compared with 8–10% in Q1 FY27.Among tier-1 cities, Pune was the only market to grow, recording a modest 2% increase, while all other metros saw demand decline. Hyderabad and Mumbai recorded the steepest declines among metros, at approximately 10% and 9%, respectively.India’s GCC workforce is projected to reach 2.7–2.8 million by 2030.

articles.title: India opens deepwater oil, gas bids, offers to fund up to 50% of well costs
articles.summary:
The government is rolling out a special licensing round for deepwater and ultra-deepwater oil and gas blocks, offering monthly bidding windows and relaxed fiscal terms as it prepares to shoulder up to 50 per cent of eligible exploratory well costs under its Rs 84,084-crore Samudra Manthan offshore exploration programme.
The special round under the Open Acreage Licensing Policy (OALP) is aimed at accelerating exploration in India's offshore frontier basins by lowering entry barriers, sharing the high costs and risks of deepwater drilling, and making acreage available to investors throughout the year.
"Under the government's 'Samudra Manthan' National Offshore Exploration Scheme, a Special OALP is being introduced for fast-track award of deepwater and ultra-deepwater (DW/UDW) exploration blocks," the Directorate General of Hydrocarbons (DGH) said in a notice.
DGH said details of the bid round will be announced shortly.
The Special OALP is a key licensing and investment facilitation .

articles.title: Delhi Police Crime Branch questions CJP leaders Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka
articles.summary:
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka appeared before the Delhi Police Crime Branch on Thursday in connection with an investigation, police sources said.
The two leaders reached the Crime Branch office in Rajouri Garden around 11 am, where a team of officers is questioning them, the sources said.
They appeared before the Crime Branch in connection with two FIRs registered against them for allegedly entering the denotified protest site at Jantar Mantar on October 13.
The two FIRs, registered at Connaught Place and Parliament Street police stations, were later transferred to the Crime Branch for investigation. Both leaders were summoned to join the probe earlier as well, but they had earlier sought more time and did not appear.
The cases relate to the alleged violation of restrictions at Jantar Mantar, where CJP members had staged a protest and unfurled the national flag.
Further details are awaited.

articles.title: SC rules 24-hour arrest deadline begins from detention, not formal arrest
articles.summary:
The Supreme Court on Thursday ruled that the 24-hour constitutional deadline for producing an arrested person before a magistrate begins from the moment he is detained, and not from the time the police formally makes the arrest.
Holding that there can be no artificial distinction between 'arrest' and 'detention' for the purpose of Article 22(2) of the Constitution, a bench of Justices Ujjal Bhuyan and Atul S Chandurkar said any interpretation allowing the police to exclude the period of pre-arrest detention would be contrary to the constitutional mandate.
"The view that 24 hours begin only from the formal arrest is contrary to the constitutional mandate of Article 22(2) and Section 56 of the BNSS," the bench observed.
The verdict that the only period that can be excluded while computing the 24-hour deadline is the time reasonably required to travel from the place of arrest to the magistrate's court.

articles.title: Tata Motors, Ashok Leyland shares rocket up to 12%. Here are 2 reasons fuelling the sharp surge
articles.summary: Shares of commercial vehicle majors Ashok Leyland and Tata Motors rallied as much as 12% on Thursday after a sharp drop in oil prices, which boosted investor sentiment amid hopes of an Iran deal.In today’s session, Ashok Leyland shares rallied as much as 12% to Rs 172 on the BSE, while commercial vehicle major Tata Motors jumped 9% to Rs 440.Why are these 2 stocks rising?1.) Oil tumbles 10% in two days - Crude oil prices crashed over a percent on Thursday, extending losses from a 9% plunge in the previous session as markets assessed the implications of the Democrats' sweeping victory over Republicans in the US midterm elections.The political setback raised expectations that mounting pressure on the Republican Party could push the Trump administration toward ending the war with Iran through a negotiated settlement.Brent crude was trading at $93.51 a barrel, down more than 1%, or $1.05 in absolute terms. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude slipped 1.35% to below $87 a barrel. In the previous session, Brent futures settled $8.98, or 8.7%, lower at $94.62 a barrel, while WTI crude futures dropped $7.97, or 8.3%, to $88.12. Both benchmarks ended Wednesday at their lowest levels since August 31.Falling crude oil prices are positive for commercial vehicle (CV) manufacturers such as Ashok Leyland and Tata Motors as diesel accounts for a significant portion of fleet operators' running costs. Lower fuel prices improve the operating economics of truck and bus owners, potentially encouraging fleet expansion, replacement demand and fresh vehicle purchases. Cheaper crude also reduces input and logistics costs for automakers, supporting margins. Additionally, lower fuel prices can ease inflationary pressures and improve overall economic activity, benefiting freight movement and transportation demand.2.) Buoyant market mood - The Indian stock market opened Thursday's session on a strong note, with benchmark indices Sensex and Nifty rallying nearly 2% amid a favourable mix of global and domestic cues. Gains by Democrats in the US midterm elections, marking a setback for US President Donald Trump, along with easing crude oil prices, boosted investor sentiment and extended Dalal Street's recovery rally for a second consecutive session.The Sensex surged over 1,400 points to cross the 78,700 mark, while the Nifty 50 jumped more than 400 points to reclaim 24,350. The sharp rally added nearly Rs 8 lakh crore to the combined market capitalisation of BSE-listed companies, taking it to Rs 501 lakh crore.Broader markets also participated in the rally, with the Nifty Midcap 100 and Nifty Smallcap 250 indices gaining up to 1.5%. Meanwhile, India VIX, the market's volatility gauge, declined 2.5% to slip below the 15 mark.Among sectoral indices, Nifty Auto, Nifty Financial Services and Nifty Realty emerged as major outperformers, rising more than 2% each.With tailwinds for the economy getting stronger, the bullish trend in the market is set to continue, said VK Vijayakumar, Chief Investment Strategist at Geojit Investments. articles.title: Trump’s pain makes D-Street bulls gain! IndiGo, Asian Paints, other crude-sensitive stocks rally up to 8% as oil drops below $95
articles.summary: Shares of paint makers, airlines, tyre manufacturers and oil marketing companies (OMCs) rallied up to 8% on Thursday as oil prices plunged nearly 10%, falling below $100 per barrel after weeks. The decline came amid a major setback for US President Donald Trump, whose Republican Party lost control of both houses of Congress in the midterm elections.Brent crude futures slipped below the $95-per-barrel mark to trade under $94, while WTI crude futures fell below $87 on Thursday morning.The sharp decline in crude prices lifted sentiment towards companies that use oil as a key raw material, as well as airlines that have been grappling with elevated aviation fuel costs. Investors also cheered the prospect of lower input costs for paint and tyre makers, while easing crude prices could offer relief to oil marketing companies.Crude-sensitive stocks rallyAmong the airlines, IndiGo shares surged 7% to trade at Rs 5,489 apiece, while SpiceJet shares jumped around 5%. Paint-maker Asian Paints saw its shares rally nearly 7%, while those of peers Indigo Paints and Berger Paints jumped up to 5%.MRF shares rallied more than 4%, with each share gaining Rs 4,995 to trade at Rs 1.23 lakh apiece. Apollo Tyres and Balkrishna Industries shares jumped more than 8%. Oil marketing companies, including Hindustan Petroleum Corporation (HPCL), Bharat Petroleum Corporation (BPCL) and Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) saw their share prices jump up to 7%.Also read | Why is Dalal Street rallying today?Why are oil prices falling today?US President Donald Trump’s Republican party lost control over both the houses of Congress, the Senate and House of Representatives. This came after the US-Iran war spiked energy prices, with Americans beginning to feel the pinch in their pockets. In a lengthy post after the party’s election defeat, Vice President JD Vance acknowledged voter dissatisfaction over the war. He said this, along with rising cost of living and other factors may have led to voters’ dissatisfaction, which in turn led to Democrats’ sweeping victory in the midterm elections.One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up. So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we're going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us."Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.  There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:1) End the war2) Focus on cost of living/inflation3) Put America First4) Change our relationship to IsraelOur voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.)In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you. The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.— JD Vance (@JDVance) November 4, 2026Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a Democrat, meanwhile pledged to bring the war to an end soon. “We are going to end the war," he said at a news conference in Washington. "We have some Republicans already who have joined us in ending the war, and the Founding Fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people,” he said.This retriggered hopes for a conclusion to the Middle East conflict that has been raging since late February this year following US and Israel’s joint military strikes on Iran, killing its former supreme leader, triggering a massive surge in oil prices and rattling global stock markets.As a result, oil prices tumbled. "Markets are assessing the impact of the midterm elections to Donald Trump's next steps with the Iran war, pricing in more likelihood for the war to end," Reuters quoted June Goh, senior oil analyst at Sparta Commodities.Also read | Oil Price Today (November 5): Crude oil falls below $94 after 9% plunge on Wednesday after midterm results. More downside ahead?What lies ahead for crude sensitive stocks?With majority in both the houses with the Democrats, war-related spending approvals are likely to be trimmed and may ease off crude oil supply related challenges through the Strait of Hormuz, said  Sunny Agrawal, Head of Fundamental Research at SBI Securities. He noted that in case crude oil prices sustains below $90-100 per barrel, then the entire inflationary narrative will take back seat and this augurs well for the Indian economy and equity markets.“We believe the crude or crude derivatives and interest rate sensitive sectors are likely to be the key beneficiaries in the short to medium term. With likely recovery in rupee, FII inflows should accelerate and should be positive for large and midcaps,” the analyst further said.Disclaimer: This article has been written by Debaroti Adhikary, who is not a SEBI-registered Research Analyst or an Investment Adviser. articles.title: The midterm verdict on Trump's economy
articles.summary: Washington: President Donald Trump was publicly humbled by inflation in Tuesday's midterm elections, as rising prices provoked a blistering set of losses for Republicans in House, Senate and gubernatorial races.Most voters said that Trump's own policies had smothered growth and drove costs even higher, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of roughly 100,000 midterm voters.Also Read: Democrats vow bill to end Iran war after midterm sweepThe president's message that the fault lay with his predecessor, Democrat Joe Biden, didn't land. Americans saw prices start to climb with Trump's chaotic rash of tariffs last year, and energy costs spiked after he launched a war with Iran in February.About two-thirds of voters said Trump's own policies had fueled inflation. By contrast, only about half of 2022 midterm voters said this about Biden's policies, according to AP VoteCast.Voters in states from California to Mississippi were broadly in agreement that Trump's taxes on foreign imports have done more harm than good.The election results matched what voters had been telling pollsters for months, but Trump had campaigned with a decidedly deaf ear."I've done a great job," Trump said at one of his final midterm rallies in Iowa. "Prices are coming way down."Voters have buyer's remorse with TrumpDemocratic victories in Tuesday's midterms signaled that most voters don't believe the economy or Trump is working for them.Consumer prices are up 3.7% over the past 12 months, compared to an inflation rate of 3% when Trump began his second term. The president told reporters on Wednesday that the Iran war "drove the gasoline up a little bit short-term," but he felt the choice to fight Iran was worth it because of its push for nuclear weapons. "If I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again," he said.There is no guarantee that a House and Senate with a Democratic majority can fix an economy pestered by uncomfortably high inflation. Trump and Congress would likely need to work on a bipartisan basis, or simply keep the economy stable enough to allow the Federal Reserve to ratchet down inflation through its setting of interest rates.But voters did prefer Democrats to the status quo of a president who could govern with little to no congressional pushback from Republicans.About 9 in 10 voters said the cost of living was a "crucial" or "major" factor in their vote for Congress. And about 6 in 10 of this group backed Democratic candidates in their local House races.The economy is still growing, but AI is a source of fear instead of hopeThe underlying economy is stronger than many Americans think, with the S&P 500 stock index up more than 10% so far this year and the unemployment rate at a healthy 4.2%. Investors greeted the news of Democratic wins as a positive with stocks up on Wednesday.Still, the major driver of growth has been the buildout of artificial intelligence - a boom that Trump has actively stoked by refusing to codify more aggressive federal oversight.Voters don't share Trump's optimism about AI, which he has renamed "super intelligence" in federal documents.Instead of buying the arguments that AI would increase productivity and accelerate growth, about 6 in 10 voters said AI will do more to hurt society.The technology could displace workers as jobs get automated or it could be a financial bubble that if popped could wreak havoc on retirement savings. Despite the anxiety, only about one-quarter of voters said AI was a "crucial" factor.Wealth isn't trickling down to the middle classTech billionaires such as Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Elon Musk have become frequent guests of Trump, attending state dinners or jetting aboard with the president. But the growing concentration of wealth has been disconcerting for voters.Nationwide, about 7 in 10 voters said the economy favors the wealthy, while only about 3 in 10 said it's fair to everyday Americans. The wealth gap has become so extreme that even a majority of voters with a 2025 household income of $300,000 or more in the tech-heavy state of California felt the economy was tilted toward the rich.Still, a slight majority of voters across the country had a "somewhat" or "very" favorable impression of capitalism, compared to about one-third who "strongly" or "somewhat" favor socialism.But the election suggested that voters believe the government should use its heft to help reduce the cost of healthcare. About 6 in 10 said they wanted the government to play a "bigger role" in addressing medical expenses. Most voters said Trump's policies have made healthcare costs worse.Trump caught in a trap with votersHow voters felt about the overall economy generally depended on the size of their paychecks. While Trump campaigned on stats suggesting record low poverty, the working poor saw their own finances as crumbling.For those earning less than $50,000 a year, about 6 in 10 said they were worse off now than they were two years ago before Trump became president.People with higher incomes felt better about the economy, but that created a different problem for Trump. Higher-income voters were more concerned about the state of American democracy, and voters focused on democracy overwhelmingly broke for Democrats. Without congressional approval, Trump laid off thousands of federal workers, altered federal spending and imposed hundreds of billions of dollars in new tariffs that the Supreme Court earlier this year ruled were illegal.About 4 in 10 households with 2025 household incomes above $200,000 said that democracy was their top issue, putting the issue about even with the economy. Voters in most lower-income categories, on the other hand, clearly prioritized the economy.Overall, a slim majority of voters said government corruption was a crucial factor for their vote, while about half said this about high prices. Higher-income voters were much less likely than lower-income voters to see high prices as a key factor.What most voters took away from the past 22 months of Trump's presidency was that he brokered deals, took government stakes in private companies and acted in ways that put him at the center of the economy instead of America's workers.Most voters - about 6 in 10 - said Trump's priorities were misplaced.When voters were asked if Trump fought for people like them, most said he didn't.

articles.title: India announces extension of $500 million line of credit for Guyana
articles.summary:
India has announced an extension of a USD 500 million line of credit for roads, health and defence projects in Guyana as External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar met Guyanese President Irfaan Ali in Antigua and Barbuda.
Jaishankar, who arrived in St. John's on Tuesday, met President Ali on the sidelines of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting on Wednesday.
"Delighted to meet with President Dr Irfaan Ali of Guyana. @presidentaligy. Reviewed the steady progress in our bilateral cooperation, especially after PM  @narendramodi's visit in 2024," Jaishankar posted on social media on Wednesday.

Trump's midterm loss dims N Korea hopes
articles.summary: Seoul: A meeting between Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un appears increasingly unlikely when the US president travels to Asia in November, analysts say, after he suffered a crushing midterm election defeat.Trump had said he "may" meet Kim this month and that it "would be exciting", but appeared to backtrack in October, saying, "I don't know... I'm not sure that anybody's asking for a meeting," while adding that his "relationship with Kim Jong Un is very good."Trump's focus on Kim and his scaling back of joint US-South Korean military drills have alarmed Asian allies, while sparking speculation that he is seeking a foreign policy win as his war with Iran stalls.Also Read: Trump renews push for permanent daylight saving time, urges Senate to pass Sunshine Protection ActBut Kim's powerful sister Kim Yo Jong signalled on Wednesday that there was little appetite for renewed dialogue with Washington, saying Pyongyang had "no need to sit face to face with such unreliable and hostile persons"."The choice for peace includes dialogue of course, but this is not surely equated with national interests for us," she said.Kim Yo Jong's comments came after the FBI accused North Korea of a $6 billion heist from cryptocurrency exchange Binance -- allegations she had previously slammed as "a grave political provocation".Kim's statement marked "a shift from defence to offence", said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University's Institute for Far Eastern Studies in South Korea."The latest statement uses the (cyberattack) issue as an opportunity to condemn the entire US policy of pressure against North Korea," he told AFP.Also Read: Democrats' US midterm sweep may give India more room to negotiate a balanced trade deal with TrumpIn 2019, North Korea's Kim Jong Un made a 60-hour train journey home from Hanoi empty-handed after a summit with Trump collapsed.Now, the dynamic has reversed. Trump is making repeated overtures, only to be met with reluctance from Pyongyang."For Kim Jong Un, maintaining the status quo is the best option right now," Lim said.Weakened TrumpAnalysts say the North Korean leader has even less incentive to meet Trump after his Republican party suffered a thumping defeat in the US midterm elections on November 3.Voters handed control of Congress to the Democrats in a stunning rebuke to Trump, leaving him as a lame duck president for the remaining two years of his term."Trump is expected to continue pursuing top-down dialogue with North Korea", said Yang Moo-jin, former president of the South's University of North Korean Studies.But Washington's "divided government and Trump's lame-duck status will be an important variable for North Korea".Pyongyang will be sceptical of Washington's ability to deliver lasting concessions, said Michael Bosack, founding director of the Parley Policy Institute and a former UN Command official."The Kim regime is looking for substantial and durable changes in US policy towards North Korea. Right now, nothing Trump offers comes with a guarantee that it will last beyond January 2029," Bosack told AFP, referring to the date when the US president's second term ends.Kim's deepening ties with Russia and China have also strengthened his position and reduced his incentive to engage with Washington.North Korea's economy grew more than three percent for a third straight year in 2025, Seoul's central bank estimated in July, citing Pyongyang's "expansion of economic cooperation with Russia" as its major driver.Nuclear ambitionsEven if Trump and Kim agree to meet, their differences over North Korea's nuclear weapons programme remain a major obstacle to any breakthrough.Pyongyang has repeatedly made clear it is no longer prepared to discuss denuclearisation.Kim Yo Jong said in September that the country's nuclear-armed status was "absolute", calling those hoping for denuclearisation "idiots".It came as South Korea's dovish President Lee Jae Myung -- who has repeatedly offered Pyongyang talks without preconditions -- suggested Washington seek a freeze, rather than the immediate elimination, of the North's nuclear programme and offer sanctions relief in return.That approach would face significant obstacles following Trump's midterm defeat though, with Democrats committed to denuclearisation and Congress holding powers over sanctions relief."Pyongyang retains negative memories of failing to make progress in negotiations under the Biden administration because of its position that there would be no sanctions relief or dialogue without prior denuclearisation measures," Kyungnam University's Lim said.North Korea's distrust of Washington, coupled with the uncertainty surrounding any agreement with Trump, could boost its nuclear ambitions."North Korea's belief that independently advancing its nuclear arsenal, regardless of changes in US administrations or political parties, was the right and strategically sound decision will be further reinforced," Lim said.Pyongyang has carried out a flurry of weapons tests in recent weeks, including trials of cluster-bomb warheads, attack drones, a precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile."The development, testing and training of new weapons will become regular and routine activities," Lim predicted.

AI stocks retreat as Democratic sweep puts data centre boom in focus
articles.summary: Wall Street's rally following the Democratic sweep of Congress did not extend to several companies riding the AI boom. Data centre builders and related technology stocks fell on Wednesday as investors weighed the possibility of greater political scrutiny of the industry's rapid expansion, Bloomberg reports.CoreWeave, Iren and Nebius declined, while power equipment makers GE Vernova and Vertiv also came under pressure. Chipmakers Nvidia and Marvell Technology slipped even as the Nasdaq 100 rose more than 1%.For live updates on US Markets, click here The election has brought concerns about rising electricity bills and AI-driven job losses into sharper focus. Meanwhile, investors were already questioning whether the industry's debt-fuelled spending can be sustained. According to Bloomberg, analysts do not expect political pressure to derail AI development, it could slow the pace of data centre expansion and investment.Also Read: Democrats’ Senate win could shield Federal Reserve from Trump’s influence, but risks persist“The Democrats will not in my opinion challenge what has already been implemented to win this race when it comes to AI. Because there is now a big competition between China and the US when it comes to technology,” Mabrouk Chetouane, Head of Global Market Strategy at Natixis Investment Managers, told Bloomberg.“Some of the questions on data centers suggested concerns about regulation should be faded, but others suggested they should remain in the spotlight. Regardless of what does or does not happen with Congress on this issue, risk does remain from the governors’ results as AI/data centers was a top issue in the close campaigns for those seats,” Lori Calvasina, Head of US Equity Strategy at RBC Capital Markets, said.“We still struggle to support the idea that the election will be a major clearing event for markets, however, given the absence of the usual turbulence in the US equity market around the election so far.”“This does add uncertainty about the path forward and maybe the pace forward, but ultimately we still think that the data center build-out will continue. Maybe the pace changes on the margin, but we ultimately think there’s huge demand for compute and that there may be some changes in how the data centers have to approach this, meaning maybe some of the tax incentives change, maybe some of the counties that really voted against this, maybe they have to move, go somewhere else. They might have to find other alternatives. But we think ultimately — much like fracking — we still expect that we see a buildout. It just may be done with some different concessions, with some guardrails, more guardrails than we had before,” Kieth Lerner, Chief Investment Officer and Chief Market Strategist at Truist Advisory Services, was quoted as saying by Bloomberg.“Republicans or Democrats sitting in any state around the country, not just Texas, look at a state that historically has been Republican friendly with a largely effective governor, seeing them overthrown on this basis that data centers are an unpopular position. I think politicians, if anything, love to get reelected before they think about policy. And so more and more, whether it be Republican or Democrat, are likely to jump on that bandwagon to air quotes protect their state from data centers. Obviously that is a popular narrative,” Brad Long, Chief Investment Officer at Wealthspire, said.“It’s certainly not going to change the fact that data centers will be built out and there’s a lot of demand and there’s a lot of backlog. The question will be the regulation and the time and the throughput there. What markets are going to have to digest is, it’s not will data centers be built, but where and how long will it take and how much red tape will be there? Which obviously pushes further out not just all the capex spending, but the throughput on the benefit from AI,” said Matt Maley, Chief Market Strategist at Miller Tabak + Co.“The headwinds are getting a little bit bigger for the AI movement. That’s going to give us some tough sledding. So it may be a lot harder for the market to see the usual year-end rally in the midterm election years. The ‘not in my backyard’ with data centers is gonna be a 2028 issue immediately, and I think that the 2028 campaign starts today. ... It is all but impossible for the Republicans to win the presidency or win the Electoral College without winning Texas,” he added.“Narrative-wise, I think the initial ‘Glass Half-Full’ post ‘Blue Tsunami’ midterm Elections -trade is based upon the following rationalizations—some probably obvious, some more nuanced: A belief that the election results will lead to a forced moderation of US datacenter buildout, which then calms concerns around the Hyperscaler Capex race-to-infinity ‘prisoner’s dilemma’…Which from a markets-perspective reduces some of financing concerns around magnitude of credit and equities issuance, slows the “FCF burn” -trajectory fears,” said Charlie McElligott, Cross Asset Strategist at Nomura Holdings Inc.“There’s definitely some fears about what this might mean for the AI build-out, especially on data centers, and those names have already been under pressure because of the expected Democratic victory. But I think it’s probably a little bit overblown. It’s going to put more onus on the states, but I don’t think that that will impact existing projects all that much. But it could result in higher cost of production if these companies have to provide maybe more local assistance or navigate more regulation across the board just to get some of these projects through. But we still need these data centers,” JP Powers, Chief Investment Officer at RWA Wealth Partners, told Bloomberg.“You could read this as a vote against data centers, but at some level there’s a lot of momentum toward building them, there’s a lot of jobs at stake. The boulder’s already rolling down the hill to some extent, so the election of a few governors and a change in Congress is not going to completely stop the momentum,” Steve Sosnick, Chief Strategist at Interactive Brokers, said.“The market’s been expressing very valid fears that the money is just being spent too aggressively and that the borrowing is so extreme. And so maybe this slows it down to something that’s a bit more manageable, which isn’t great for the suppliers, but may actually impose a little financial discipline on the industry that markets are okay with.”“This is a wake up call. They have to really get out and make their case why communities should want data centers. I think in the end they will be successful, but it probably slows some of these projects down,” Peter Tchir, Head of Macro Strategy at Academy Securities, said.“Gov-elect Hinojosa favors an immediate moratorium on data center builds in Texas until new laws can be passed to establish guardrails. One interpretation is that existing builds / permits would be free to continue and all new construction would be halted and thus would move to other states. Another interpretation is that the datacenter build is slowing and likely reducing capex; this theme had been building into the election,” Andrew Tyler, Head of Global Market Intelligence at JPMorgan Chase & Co., told Bloomberg. “We would not abandon the Tech trade and would play for a tactical rebound, but we may see the market become increasingly selective of Tech / AI winners and losers.” (Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)

articles.title: Crude cools, but war risks keeps mkts guessing
articles.summary: New Delhi: Oil prices may remain elevated as President Donald Trump's weakened political position after the midterms complicates efforts to end the Iran war and Tehran grows more emboldened, industry executives said, although crude oil cooled hours after the results came out.Brent futures dropped $9.27, or 8.9%, to $94.29 a barrel, touching the lowest level since September 4. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down $7.44, or 7.8%, to $88.54.Also read: And quiet flows the Don: Trump goes from rage to rapproachementTrump could seek to demonstrate strength by intensifying military operations against Iran, but Democrats' control of Congress could constrain his ability to fund the war in West Asia. "Trump has already lost the midterms and cannot seek re-election. To prove the American public that he is right, he may escalate the military conflict," an executive said.Since the war began, Trump has pursued two objectives: intensifying military pressure on Iran while keeping oil prices in check, often by signalling that the conflict was nearing an end and would not escalate. With the elections behind him, he may be more willing to let oil prices rise in the short term and focus on achieving his military objectives.A decisive outcome, whether through military action or a deal, would be preferable to the prolonged stalemate that has imposed heavy costs on oil importers, executives said. But an escalation involving ground forces could also prolong the conflict, further disrupting energy supplies and raising costs for consumers.A deal with Iran could offer Trump a way to claim victory while bringing down oil prices and easing the cost-of-living pressures that contributed to the Republicans' defeat. However, a settlement that allows Iran to impose a permanent toll on shipping through Hormuz could undermine Trump's ambition to be remembered as one of America's greatest presidents, another executive said.Also read: Trump admits Iran war hurt Republicans in midterms but says ‘Iran thing’ had to be doneIndian refiners would ideally prefer unrestricted passage through Hormuz, an executive said.Whether or not Iran is allowed to levy a toll, a resolution that restores the flow of oil through the strait would reduce the risk premium on crude prices and bring down freight rates, lowering procurement costs for importers such as India, he said.Brent crude is near $100 a barrel, while freight and insurance costs are several times higher than before the war. Brent was around $70 before the war started.The cost of the prolonged disruption has been compounded by uncertainty over the reliability of supplies. Although oil flows through the strait have risen sharply in the past two months, they remain expensive and unpredictable, making the current situation unsustainable for importers."This is better than no flows at all but definitely not sustainable," an executive said.

articles.title: Don Trump goes from rage to rapproachement
articles.summary: TOI Correspondent From Washington: The man who posts on social media at the drop of a hat, at all times and at odd hours, sometimes a dozen posts an hour, was rendered rather speechless after an electoral thrashing for the ages.Now a lame-duck President for all purposes but still armed with enormous executive powers, Donald Trump reacted to the Republican rout first with a mix of denial and defiance, and later with nonchalance and some conciliation. His initial reaction when the Democratic demolistion came into view early on Tuesday night was one of denial. “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” he posted on his propaganda platform “Truth Social.”Track US Senate Elections Result 2026 Live Updates hereThen it was a couple of rage posts about Fox News -- his favored propaganda network whose coverage became funereal as the night wore on -- and blaming Republican candidates, including defeated Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a wheelchair-bound GOP stalwart who was thwarted in his bid for a third term.“If Greg Abbott hadn’t become a RINO (Republican in Name Only) in the last six months of his Political Life, he wouldn’t have lost. He went back to his original formula, and it wasn’t pretty!” he wrote, throwing the veteran under the bus and absolving himself of all blame. He told Fox News that some voters simply “didn’t like the candidates.”Shortly after midnight, he posted a photo of a red baseball cap with the word VETO on it – suggesting that he will simply block any Democrat-written bills, creating a deadlock since Dems do not have the 2/3rds majority in both chambers to override a presidential veto.Then he went silent for more than nine hours, but not before he also told a C-Span in a live phone call that he would work with Democrats and not veto everything they sent, even though he has the right to do so.Also read: US midterm elections 2026: Democrats sweep House and Senate, deal Trump major blow"We're going to work with the Democrats, to make sure things go well for our country... We have a lot of friends in the Democratic Party,” he said in a conciliatory tone at odds with his familiar combativeness.Democrats too have every reason to work with the President. The U.S Constitution (Article I, Section 7) requires a two-thirds majority vote in both the House of Representatives (290/435) and the Senate (67/100) to overcome the veto – although the qualifier is 2/3rds majority of those “present and voting." Dems are well short of that double which last occurred in 1965 during the Lyndon Johnson Presidency.But a testing time is afoot even within the Republican ranks. The rout shocked and angered many conservatives, some of whom began to turn on Trump publicly. “Dems look like they might get 56 (Senate seats).. Rs will never get that back for a long time. You ignore primaries for years, anoint a charlatan as not just leader but God, and then mimic his retardation every day for a decade, at some point the chickens come home to roost,” raged Daniel Horowitz, a commentator at the right leaning outlet The Blaze. "It's on him. It's not on anybody else. It's a total, complete rejection of President Trump," Bill Miller, a top Republican lobbyist in Texas, told BBC, calling it “a disaster of the first magnitude” that nobody saw coming.Also read: US Vice President JD Vance says Iran war is 'the reason we lost' midterms 2026Actually, every poll and survey other than MAGA affiliated ones saw it coming, although the scale was not foreseen by most. In fact, Democrats went to polling day wary of the “too good to be true” projections given past setbacks, particularly in 2016 when Trump himself did not appear to believe he would win. This time around, he tried to conjure up victory in the face of imminent defeat with bravado and bluster, but voters had other ideas. They trussed him up by giving Democrats a comfortable majority in both chambers of Congress.

articles.title: Correction? AI stocks tumble post midterms
articles.summary: US stock market update: Dow Jones rallies today after Democrats win Congress - Democrats have won both the Senate and the House, and the stock market liked it. By 10:44 am ET on Wednesday, the Dow Jones was up 1,245 points, or 2.40%, at 53,032. The S&P 500 rose 1.52% and the Nasdaq gained 1.82%. But not every stock joined in. Data centre companies, Tesla and SpaceX fell. Democrats made gains in Texas and Georgia, where public opposition to new data centres is growing, and investors fear tighter rules could slow the AI boom.Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Governor Greg Abbott after promising an immediate pause on new data centre projects until lawmakers introduce stronger safeguards. The result added to pressure on AI infrastructure stocks, with CoreWeave falling 7%.The concern is significant because Texas accounts for an estimated 27% of planned US data centre capacity, according to Wells Fargo.Will a Democratic Congress slow the AI boom? Why data center stocks fell as the Dow gained 1,100 points The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 2.13% to 52,889.71, gaining 1,102.99 points. The S&P 500 climbed 1.49% to 7,681.76, while the Nasdaq Composite advanced 1.97% to 25,871.41.ALSO READ: US stock market stages big rally today: Why is Dow Jones surging? Dow jumps 1,100 points as S&P 500 and Nasdaq turn green, with healthcare stocks at the centreWith Republicans losing control of both chambers of Congress, President Donald Trump's administration could face greater difficulty passing major policy changes.Investors also saw the election outcome as a way to reduce uncertainty. Markets had been watching closely for the results because changes in Congress could affect tariffs, government spending, energy policy and regulations.Scott Chornert, head of US equity strategy at Citi Research, described the election as a clearing event, suggesting that investors could now move beyond the uncertainty surrounding the vote.Amazon was among the strongest performers in the technology sector. Its shares gained around 7.1%, while Alphabet rose 3.4% and Meta Platforms added 1.6%.Other major technology stocks also moved higher. Apple and Microsoft gained nearly 6% in morning trading, according to market reports.McDonald's also climbed around 3.9% after reporting quarterly profits above market expectations. Amgen gained about 3% following its results.Block shares jumped 15% after the payments company raised its full-year gross profit outlook.Tesla and SpaceX sharesElon Musk's companies moved in the opposite direction. SpaceX shares fell around 1.9% to $138.91 in the supplied market data, while Tesla declined nearly 4% in morning trading.Musk had spent heavily backing Republican candidates during the election campaign. The Democratic victories could bring greater scrutiny of some of his business interests, particularly government contracts, artificial intelligence and the proposed merger between Tesla and SpaceX.AI and data centre stocks face fresh pressureThe election results also brought attention to the future of the US artificial intelligence industry.Democrats made gains in states such as Texas and Georgia, where local opposition to the rapid expansion of data centres has been growing.Data centres require large amounts of electricity, land and water. Their expansion has raised concerns about power costs, local infrastructure and the impact on nearby communities.Investors are now considering whether tighter rules could delay new projects and affect companies supplying equipment and computing services.Shares of data centre operators, including IREN, Hut 8, Applied Digital and Core Scientific, fell between 1.2% and 13%.Nvidia shares slipped 0.41% in the supplied market snapshot, while AMD gained around 4.8% after issuing a stronger growth outlook for 2027.Solar stocks rise while defence shares fallClean energy companies were among the biggest beneficiaries of the election outcome.The Invesco Solar ETF jumped 8.3% as investors considered the possibility that federal support for solar and other clean energy projects would remain in place.Defence stocks moved lower. Northrop Grumman and Lockheed Martin each lost more than 4% in morning trading.The change followed concerns that a Democratic-controlled Congress could make it harder for Trump to secure approval for his proposed $1.5 trillion defence budget.Palantir also fell around 1% amid concerns about its exposure to government and defence contracts.Oil falls while gold and cryptocurrencies move higherWTI crude oil fell 2.31% to $93.87 a barrel, while Brent crude declined 2.27% to $101.25. Investors were watching developments surrounding the US-Israeli war on Iran and its possible impact on oil supplies and inflation.Gold futures rose 2.53% to $4,040.10 an ounce. Silver gained 4.40% to $51.94.Cryptocurrencies also moved higher. Bitcoin rose 3.69% to $80,500.84, while Ether gained 6.68% to $2,433.23. XRP advanced 3.01% to $1.32.The US 10-year Treasury yield also moved lower, falling to 4.93% from 4.97% in the previous session.

articles.title: Aswath Damodaran trims his Anthropic IPO valuation to $1.45 trillion; Dean of valuation explains why
articles.summary: Valuation expert Aswath Damodaran trimmed his valuation estimate for AI giant Anthropic to $1.45 trillion, from his earlier estimate of $1.475 trillion which was already lower than the industry estimates of $2 trillion.The 'Dean of Valuation' in a long blogpost said his earlier valuation estimate which was lower than the overall market view received strong reactions. Some of them were solely based on emotion, he said, as they held strong conviction in the company. Some of it was based on cost of capital, which the analyst believes reflects a fundamental disconnect with market history, current market pricing and basic business sense.Also read | Dean of valuation Aswath Damodaran pegs Anthropic's worth at $1.475 trillion ahead of mega IPOHis latest $1.45 trillion valuation accounts for the trailing 12-month revenue and operating income numbers to include the just-leaked third quarter numbers. “The equity value that I obtain for Anthropic is close to the lower end of the offering price estimates, but as I noted at the time that I posted it, and will reinforce again now, it is a function of not just my upbeat story about the company, but also one about how the AI products and services market will evolve over time,” he wrote.Aswath Damodaran’s worries for AnthropicDamodaran estimates Anthropic’s target revenues will reach a trillion dollars in ten years. Not only would this put them at or close to the top of all companies, in terms of total annual revenues, but they will also be sharing that grouping with companies like Amazon and Walmart that deliver on scale, but at the expense of margins, he said, adding that Anthropic emerges as a winner in the premium portion of the AI market, capturing a dominant market share, with pricing power.In his previous post valuing Anthropic, Damodaran had raised the alarm over the company’s governance structure, stating that its structure as a public benefit corporation and a voting share concoction that leaves founders in control, no matter how much capital the company raises in equity markets. He said he received feedback that this may not be a negative as these are smart people who know AI better than the rest. The analyst is however not convinced as he believes concentration of power in the hands of founders is a bad idea.Also read | Aswath Damodaran explains why country risk is no longer just an emerging market problem“While much of the focus on Anthropic has been on their compute commitments, disclosed (loosely) in their prospectus, my valuation of Anthropic is driven by expectations of what those commitments will look like over time, and especially if my growth story for the company comes into fruition. Delivering a trillion dollars of revenues will require Anthropic to not just maintain and replenish the compute power that it has already locked down, but add to that power over time,” Damodaran said, warning that building new data centers is getting more difficult, as local communities push back, and politicians realize that opposing them is a net vote winnerRegulatory risks are also one of the key worries for Anthropic. “Put simply, Anthropic will become riskier, if revenues do not measure up to expectations and the pathway to profitability becomes rockier, making it more an output than an input variable,” the valuation expert said.How investors should react to Anthropic’s IPO?While Damodaran remains cautious about Anthropic’s IPO, he noted that uncertainty is a feature of investing, no matter what one invests in, with the differences across investments lying in how much uncertainty one face, rather than whether she faces.Also read | AI boom heading for a dot-com-style bust? ‘Dean of Valuation’ Aswath Damodaran warns correction could be more painful than 2008He listed out four responses to such uncertainties.1) Ignore it: Damodaran pointed out that there are investors who are capable of ignoring uncertainty and going in fully even on the most uncertain investments. They are able to do so because they are far less risk averse than the rest and are willing to live with the consequences of investments (and their portfolios) blowing up. “They are more gamblers than investors, but with good instincts and timing, gamblers can get wealthy too,” he said.2) Avoid it: If an investor completely wants to avoid uncertainty, she cannot invest in equities, corporate bonds, which have risk of default, and even treasury bonds, which have price risk from shifting interest rates, Damodaran noted. Unless the investor simply wants to just hold cash, she has to therefore decide what her threshold for risk is, and stay within that threshold.3) Margin of Safety: The third approach to dealing with uncertainty also borrows from conventional value investing and imposing a margin of safety, where you will buy a stock only if its price is less than your value estimate by a margin (20%, 30%, 40%) that you specify.4) Law of large numbers: “If I had a million dollars in investable funds, would I invest that entire amount in Anthropic, even if it trades at well below my assessed value? The answer would be no, given the uncertainties associated with the future of the company, but that answer would change if my portfolio became less concentrated, since its performance would be less a function of any individual company's performance (good or bad),” Damodaran said. In effect, he said he is using the law of large numbers as an ally to not only reduce his risk exposure to individual companies, but also as a basis for making investments in far riskier stocks than he would be otherwise inclined to invest in.Disclaimer: This article has been written by Debaroti Adhikary, who is not a SEBI-registered Research Analyst or an Investment Adviser.
